blocks.text: When two tennis balls collide, after the collision they rebound with velocities less than those before the impact: a portion of the kinetic energy is lost, partly through friction as the molecules in the ball move past one another when the balls distort, and partly through its change into heat and sound energy.

blocks.title: Inelastic and perfectly elastic collisions
blocks.text: A collision in which the kinetic energy of the system is not conserved is called an inelastic collision. Under certain special conditions no kinetic energy is lost; in the ideal case when no kinetic energy is lost the collision is said to be perfectly elastic. For example, a hard ball dropped onto a marble floor rebounds to very nearly its initial height, losing a negligible amount of energy in the collision with the floor. Momentum and total energy are conserved in all types of collision; kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.

Consider two smooth, non-rotating balls of masses m1 and m2 moving initially with velocities v1 and v2 in the same direction. They collide and afterwards move along the same straight line without rotation, with velocities v1' and v2' (Fig. 2.10). Taking the positive direction of velocity and momentum to the right, the law of conservation of momentum gives m1 v1 + m2 v2 = m1 v1' + m2 v2', or m1 (v1 - v1') = m2 (v2' - v2) ... (2.29). As the collision is elastic the kinetic energy is conserved: (1/2) m1 v1^2 + (1/2) m2 v2^2 = (1/2) m1 v1'^2 + (1/2) m2 v2'^2, or m1 (v1^2 - v1'^2) = m2 (v2'^2 - v2^2), or m1 (v1 + v1')(v1 - v1') = m2 (v2' + v2)(v2' - v2) ... (2.30). Dividing Eq. (2.30) by (2.29): v1 + v1' = v2' + v2 ... (2.31), or v1 - v2 = v2' - v1' = -(v1' - v2'). Before the collision v1 - v2 is the velocity of the first ball relative to the second, and v1' - v2' is the relative velocity after; so the relative velocities before and after the collision have the same magnitude but are reversed: the magnitude of the relative velocity of approach equals the magnitude of the relative velocity of separation.

In (2.29) and (2.30) m1, m2, v1 and v2 are known; solving for the unknowns v1' and v2' gives v1' = ((m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2)) v1 + (2 m2/(m1 + m2)) v2 ... (2.32) and v2' = (2 m1/(m1 + m2)) v1 + ((m2 - m1)/(m1 + m2)) v2 ... (2.33).

items: When m1 = m2: from (2.32) and (2.33), v1' = v2 and v2' = v1 (Fig. 2.11): the balls exchange velocities.

When m1 = m2 and v2 = 0: with m2 at rest, (2.32) and (2.33) give v1' = 0 and v2' = v1: the ball m1 comes to a stop and m2 takes off with the velocity m1 originally had (Fig. 2.12), as when a billiard ball moving on a table collides with an exactly similar ball at rest.

When a light body collides with a massive body at rest: v2 = 0 and m2 is much greater than m1, so m1 can be neglected compared with m2, and (2.32) and (2.33) give v1' = -v1 and v2' = 0 (Fig. 2.13): m1 bounces back with the same velocity while m2 remains stationary, a fact used by the squash player.

When a massive body collides with a light stationary body: m1 much greater than m2 and v2 = 0, so m2 is neglected in (2.32) and (2.33), giving v1' approximately v1 and v2' approximately 2 v1 (Fig. 2.14): practically no change in the velocity of the massive body, but the lighter one bounces off forward with approximately twice the velocity of the incident body.

blocks.caption: Momentum, impulse, collisions and rocket propulsion (original diagram after Figures 2.9 to 2.18 and topics 2.7 to 2.12).
blocks.long_description: Momentum is mass times velocity, and the force on a body equals the rate at which its momentum changes, so the impulse of a force, its product with the time it acts, equals the change in momentum. In an isolated system the equal and opposite forces between two colliding bodies change their momenta by equal and opposite amounts, so the total momentum is unchanged. In an elastic head-on collision kinetic energy is also conserved, the relative velocity of separation equals the relative velocity of approach, equal masses exchange velocities, a light ball rebounds from a heavy one at rest, and a heavy ball drives a light one off at about twice its own speed. In a glancing elastic collision momentum is conserved along and across the line of approach while kinetic energy is conserved as a scalar. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together, the common velocity follows from momentum, and a fraction of the kinetic energy equal to the target's share of the total mass is lost. A rocket gains momentum equal and opposite to that of the gas it ejects, so its acceleration is the mass ejected per second times the gas velocity divided by the rocket's mass, which rises as fuel is used.

blocks.title: Example 2.8
blocks.text: A 70 g ball collides with another ball of mass 140 g. The initial velocity of the first ball is 9 m s^-1 to the right while the second is at rest. If the collision were perfectly elastic, what would be the velocities of the two balls after it? Solution: m1 = 70 g, v1 = 9 m s^-1, v2 = 0, m2 = 140 g. v1' = ((m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2)) v1 = ((70 g - 140 g)/(70 g + 140 g)) x 9 m s^-1 = -3 m s^-1; v2' = (2 m1/(m1 + m2)) v1 = (2 x 70 g/(70 g + 140 g)) x 9 m s^-1 = 6 m s^-1.

blocks.prompt: Differentiate an elastic from an inelastic collision, and explain why a squash ball rebounds from the wall at almost its incoming speed (short question 2.3; case iii).
blocks.explanation: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound or deformation. Total energy and momentum are conserved in both. The ball is light and the wall massive and at rest, so with m1 negligible against m2 the formulae give v1' = -v1 and v2' = 0: the ball bounces back with the same speed and the wall stays put.

items: Inelastic: kinetic energy not conserved; perfectly elastic: no kinetic energy lost. Momentum and total energy are conserved in every collision.

Head-on elastic: m1 (v1 - v1') = m2 (v2' - v2); v1 + v1' = v2 + v2' (approach speed = separation speed); v1' = ((m1 - m2)/(m1 + m2)) v1 + (2 m2/(m1 + m2)) v2, v2' = (2 m1/(m1 + m2)) v1 + ((m2 - m1)/(m1 + m2)) v2; four special cases. Example 2.8: -3 and 6 m s^-1.
